title: Going Places
summary: Sophie, a school-leaver from a working-class family, dreams of glamour: owning a boutique, becoming an actress or a fashion designer, and meeting her hero, the young Irish footballer Danny Casey. A. R. Barton’s story contrasts her fantasies with the practical outlook of her friend Jansie and shows the pain of adolescent hero-worship when dreams collide with reality.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: A. R. Barton is a modern English writer who has lived in Germany and Spain. His stories often explore the inner world of young people and the gap between aspiration and reality.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Sophie and Jansie are about to leave school and are destined for the local biscuit factory. Sophie refuses to accept this and talks of grand careers. At home, amid her tired mother, sarcastic father and little brother Derek, she claims she met Danny Casey in the arcade and that he has promised to meet her. Her silent elder brother Geoff half-believes her. On the evening of the supposed meeting, she waits alone by the canal under the trees, but Danny never comes. She is left with sadness and the fear that her family will not believe her.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
Sophie’s dreams. Walking home with Jansie, Sophie announces that she will open a boutique when she leaves school. Jansie reminds her that it needs money and that they are both going to the biscuit factory. Sophie then talks of being a manager, an actress or a fashion designer. Jansie’s practical replies cannot puncture her dreams.

Life at home. Sophie’s family lives in a cramped house. Her mother is worn out with housework, her father is a heavy, sweating labourer who loves football, and her younger brother Derek is cheeky. Her elder brother Geoff, an apprentice mechanic, is quiet and distant. Sophie idolises Geoff and longs to share his world, imagining the exciting places and people he must know.

The Danny Casey story. Sophie tells Geoff that she met Danny Casey, the young Irish football prodigy of United, in the arcade, and that he signed her autograph book, though she had no paper and he wrote nothing. She says he promised to meet her. Geoff is doubtful; her father mocks her, saying she is always making up tales. Geoff warns her that Jansie may spread the story and her father will be furious.

The football match. On Saturday, Sophie goes with her family to watch United play. Danny Casey scores a brilliant goal and Sophie is thrilled, as if the triumph were partly hers.

Waiting by the canal. On the evening of the supposed date, Sophie goes to the canal, sits on a bench under the trees and waits for Danny. As time passes and darkness gathers, she realises he will not come. She imagines how she must face Geoff’s disbelief. Even so, she cannot let the dream die: in her heart Danny remains her hero. The story leaves it clear that the meeting was imagined.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Adolescent fantasy and hero-worship: Sophie’s idealisation of Danny Casey and of Geoff.
  • Dream versus reality: grand ambitions clash with the limits of a working-class background.
  • Class and economic constraints: girls like Sophie and Jansie are expected to work in the biscuit factory.
  • Loneliness and the need for recognition: Sophie wants to be noticed and admired.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Sophie: imaginative, restless and romantic. She escapes her drab surroundings through dreams and confuses fantasy with fact. Sensitive and lonely, she longs for attention, especially from Geoff. Her disappointment at the canal is touching.

Jansie: Sophie’s friend, practical and realistic. She knows their future lies in the biscuit factory and gently tries to bring Sophie down to earth. She is also inquisitive and likely to gossip.

Geoff: Sophie’s elder brother, a quiet apprentice mechanic. Reserved and mature, he lives in his own world, which fascinates Sophie.

Sophie’s father: a hard-working, blunt man who is passionate about football and dismissive of Sophie’s tales.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: ‘Going places’ is an idiom meaning becoming successful. Sophie dreams of going places in life, through glamour and fame, and her fantasy carries her to an imaginary meeting with Danny Casey. The irony is that, in reality, she is going nowhere beyond the biscuit factory, which makes the title apt and poignant.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Dreams are valuable, but they must be grounded in effort and reality. Blind hero-worship can lead to disappointment. Families should communicate with and support young people’s aspirations.

keyTerms.definition: A small shop selling fashionable clothes; Sophie’s first dream.
Excessive admiration for a person; Sophie’s attitude towards Danny Casey.
A covered passage with shops where Sophie claims she met Danny.
A person learning a trade from a skilled employer; Geoff is an apprentice mechanic.
A young person with exceptional talent; Danny Casey is described as one.
The contrast between Sophie’s dreams of ‘going places’ and her limited real prospects.

mcqs.q: Where were Sophie and Jansie expected to work after school?
mcqs.explanation: Jansie reminds Sophie that they are both marked for the biscuit factory.
Danny Casey was a young Irish footballer, a rising star of United.

mcqs.q: Why did Sophie admire her brother Geoff?
options: He seemed mysterious and lived in a world she longed to enter.
mcqs.explanation: Quiet, grown-up Geoff seemed to have an exciting world of his own that Sophie wanted to share.

mcqs.q: What was Jansie’s attitude towards Sophie’s dreams?
mcqs.explanation: Jansie was realistic and reminded Sophie of money and their future in the factory.

mcqs.q: How did Sophie’s father react to her story about meeting Danny?
options: He dismissed it as one of her fantasies.
mcqs.explanation: He mocked her, treating it as another of her made-up stories.

mcqs.q: Why could Danny not sign Sophie’s autograph, according to her story?
options: Neither of them had paper or a pen.
mcqs.explanation: Sophie said they had no paper or pen, a detail that hints the meeting was imaginary.

mcqs.q: Where did Sophie wait for Danny Casey?
options: By the canal, under the trees
mcqs.explanation: She waited on a bench by the canal as evening turned to night.

mcqs.q: What does the title ‘Going Places’ mean?
mcqs.explanation: The idiom means rising to success, which is ironic for Sophie.

mcqs.q: What did Sophie fear most after Danny failed to come?
options: Geoff’s disbelief and having to face him
mcqs.explanation: She worried about how to face Geoff, whose belief she valued most.
Geoff is an apprentice mechanic, travelling daily to work.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: Sitting alone by the canal as darkness falls, Sophie slowly understands that Danny will not come, yet she clings to the memory of his brilliant goal.
(a) Why had Sophie come to the canal? (1)
(b) What does her waiting reveal about her? (1)
(c) What does she fear now? (1)
(d) What theme does this moment highlight? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) She believed Danny Casey had promised to meet her there.

(b) It reveals that she confuses fantasy with reality and is deeply romantic.

(c) She fears facing Geoff’s disbelief.

(d) The clash between dream and reality / adolescent hero-worship.

questions.q: Why did Sophie want to share Geoff’s secret world?
questions.answerHtml: Geoff was older, quiet and went out to work, so he seemed to have exciting places and friends Sophie knew nothing about. She felt shut out and longed to be part of that adult world, to be taken seriously and included in his confidences.

questions.q: How does Jansie differ from Sophie?
questions.answerHtml: Jansie is realistic and accepts that they will work at the biscuit factory, while Sophie lives in dreams of boutiques and fame. Jansie points out practical facts like money, whereas Sophie ignores them. Jansie is also more down-to-earth and gossipy.

questions.q: Why did Sophie’s father dismiss her story of meeting Danny Casey?
questions.answerHtml: Her father knew Sophie often made up fanciful stories. A famous footballer meeting an ordinary schoolgirl in an arcade seemed impossible to him. Being practical and blunt, he mocked her and warned that such tales would get her into trouble.

questions.q: ‘Going Places’ is a story about adolescent fantasising and hero-worship. Discuss. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
‘Going Places’ captures the dreamy world of a teenager who escapes her dull reality through fantasy. Sophie, from a struggling working-class family, refuses to accept that her future lies in the biscuit factory. She imagines owning a boutique, becoming an actress or a fashion designer, without any thought of money or training.

Her hero-worship centres on Danny Casey, a young football star. She builds an elaborate story of meeting him at the arcade and arranging a date. She also idolises her brother Geoff, imagining a glamorous life for him. Watching Danny score at the match, she feels personally involved in his glory.

The fantasy collapses by the canal when Danny does not appear. Yet Sophie still clings to her dream. Through her, Barton shows how adolescents create idols to fill emotional gaps, and how this can lead to disappointment when dreams are not anchored in reality.

questions.q: Describe Sophie’s family and how it shapes her personality. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Sophie belongs to a lower-middle-class family living in a cramped house. Her mother is tired and overworked, constantly busy with chores. Her father is a hard-working labourer, heavy and blunt, whose main joy is football; he has little patience for Sophie’s tales. Her younger brother Derek is cheeky, and her elder brother Geoff, an apprentice mechanic, is quiet and reserved.

This environment affects Sophie deeply. The lack of money and opportunities makes her long for glamour and escape. Since no one takes her seriously, she craves attention and invents stories to impress. Her father’s mockery and Geoff’s distance make her feel unheard, so she turns to dreams and idols like Danny Casey.

Thus her family’s circumstances, its struggles and emotional distance, fuel both her restless imagination and her loneliness. Her fantasies are a way of coping with a world that seems to offer her very little.
